common_name: Pink Lightning Ajuga (White-Edged Mint-Green Bugleweed with Pink Flowers)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring, spacing 8-12 inches apart, in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full shade; a white-edged sport of 'Purple Torch' discovered at Sunny Border Nursery, it spreads by stolons to knit into a solid mat within one to two seasons.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Pink Lightning stands apart from most ajuga cultivars by pairing soft mint-green, crinkled foliage edged in creamy white with short spikes of bubblegum-pink flowers in mid to late spring, rather than the blue-violet blooms typical of the species. The pastel flower color and cool variegated foliage make it a useful contrast plant against the many bronze- and purple-leaved bugleweed selections. It spreads at a moderate pace by surface stolons, filling in as a dense, weed-suppressing carpet beneath shrubs and trees, and remains semi-evergreen in milder climates. Divide congested patches every few years in spring to renew vigor and keep the variegation crisp; light afternoon shade helps prevent leaf scorch in hot summer regions.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock 8-12 inches apart in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade with some sun; a touch of morning or filtered sun brings out the deepest bronze-purple foliage tones.

directions: Plant in average, rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to shade with some sun exposure; Purple Torch forms low rosettes of glossy, dark bronze-green leaves that deepen to purple-bronze in cooler weather and winter. Its signature feature is the flower display: lavender-pink blooms rise on distinctive torch-shaped spikes well above the foliage, to about 12 inches, in a color and form that stand out from the typical blue-violet ajuga flower spike. Some sun is needed to maximize the purple foliage color, though full shade under tree canopies still produces acceptable growth with more subdued tones. It spreads by stolons to form a dense mat useful for dry shade under trees, slopes, and difficult sites where turf fails, and attracts bees while in bloom. Divide crowded clumps in spring every few years to maintain vigor.
